summary: John Melmoth, a Dublin student, finds the portrait of an ancestor who sold his soul for 150 extra years of life and now roams the world looking for someone to take over the pact. The book is a set of stories nested inside one another. A Spaniard, Alonzo Monçada, tells of a monastery and the Inquisition, then a manuscript tells of Immalee, a castaway girl on an Indian Ocean island whom Melmoth tries to corrupt. No one he approaches will trade places with him, however desperate they are.
context: Charles Maturin, an Irish clergyman of the Church of Ireland, published the novel in 1820. He was under pressure from his publisher to meet a contract, which helps explain its uneven, story-by-story shape. He did much of his reading in Marsh's Library in Dublin, near his home on York Street, and built himself a desk there. The book denounces Roman Catholicism in favour of Protestantism and offers comment on England of its day. A French translation appeared in 1821, and Balzac, Baudelaire and Poe admired it. Oscar Wilde, a relation by marriage, later took the name Melmoth in exile.

people.name: Charles Maturin
people.note: Irish Protestant clergyman and Gothic writer, 1780 to 1824.

people.name: John Melmoth
people.note: Dublin student who inherits the portrait and the family story.

people.name: Melmoth the Wanderer
people.note: Scholar who traded his soul for 150 extra years of life.

people.name: Alonzo Monçada
people.note: Spaniard confined to a monastery who escapes the Inquisition and tells his tale.

people.name: Immalee / Isidora
people.note: Castaway raised alone on an island, later restored to her family in Madrid.

people.name: Stanton
people.note: Man whose manuscript describes his search for Melmoth, and who is sent to a madhouse.

people.name: Oscar Wilde
people.note: Great-nephew by marriage of Maturin, who took the name Melmoth in exile in France.

people.name: Honore de Balzac
people.note: Wrote the parody Melmoth Reconcilie in 1835.

places.name: Dublin
places.note: Home of Maturin and of the Melmoth family in the story.

places.name: Marsh's Library, Dublin
places.note: Ireland's first public library, opened in 1707, where Maturin researched the novel.

places.name: Madrid
places.note: Where Immalee, now Isidora, is restored to her family.

places.name: Loughrea
places.note: In County Galway, where Maturin was ordained curate in 1803.

places.name: Yorkshire
places.note: Home of Elinor in the Lovers' Tale.

ideas.title: Stories within stories
ideas.note: The novel is built from nested tales that slowly reveal Melmoth's life.

ideas.title: The bargain of the soul
ideas.note: Melmoth seeks someone who will take over his pact, in the manner of the Wandering Jew.

ideas.title: Innocence tested
ideas.note: Melmoth shows Immalee the failings of human societies and religions.

ideas.title: Convent and Inquisition
ideas.note: Monçada's tale presents monastic life and the Inquisition as cruelty.

ideas.title: Anti-Catholic polemic
ideas.note: The book denounces Roman Catholicism in favour of the virtues of Protestantism.

passages.quote: I am a very poor man. I never troubled a clergyman before, and all I want is, that you will grant me two trifling requests, very little matters in your way⁠—save my soul, and (whispering) make interest to get me a parish coffin⁠—I have not enough left to bury me.
passages.why: A dying man's plain request to a clergyman, early in the book.

passages.quote: Immalee, for that was the name her votarists had given her, was standing on the shore, when a being approached her unlike any she had ever beheld.
passages.why: Immalee on the shore sees Melmoth for the first time.

passages.why: Immalee tells Melmoth that she feels pain only since he came.

passages.quote: I have traversed the world in the search, and no one, to gain that world, would lose his own soul!
passages.why: Melmoth's failure: no one will lose his soul to gain the world.
